tools.name: run_monte_carlo_simulation
tools.description: Runs a Monte Carlo simulation of a model and returns the full range of possible outcomes of every result, not one guessed number; for only a worst, median and best case or one percentile such as P80, summarize_outcome_scenarios answers directly, and to find which input moves an outcome most, use rank_inputs_by_impact. A model is a set of uncertain inputs, the formulas that combine them, and the links between them. The simulation draws random values for every input many times; each draw is a trial, and one call is one run. Use this when you need to know how likely different outcomes are for a plan built on uncertain inputs: a project's total cost or budget (for example from low / most likely / high estimates per line item), a schedule or delivery date, capacity, revenue, or an investment's NPV, IRR or payback. It returns a summary for each output node. By default the output nodes are the model's end results: every node that no other node takes as an input, such as a total cost. If you list nodes in run_params.output_request.nodes, exactly those are reported instead. For each one it gives the mean, the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles (the value that share of trials fall below), the minimum and maximum in the last time period, and the same per period; plus any metrics you asked for, such as NPV, IRR, payback or the chance of beating a target or budget; and a run_id. Pass that run_id to get_simulation_results for other nodes, periods or percentiles. Give the model in exactly one of two ways: inline in graph, or as the graph_id of a model saved with save_graph (no need to read it first). Sending both, or neither, is refused with validation_error and costs nothing. Every input needs a distribution before a run: an inline model with an input whose distribution_type is still null or left empty is refused with validation_error and not run (check_simulation_model, which never runs, lists that input as an issue instead). So do not call this tool for a model the user wants to finish later, even when they ask to run it inline now: tell the user which input still needs a distribution, or keep the unfinished model with save_graph. trials sets how many trials this run draws (a trial count), for this run only, inline or saved, and never changes a saved model: to run saved model 8f3c2a with 50,000 trials, call this tool once with {"graph_id":"8f3c2a","trials":50000}. To change anything else in a saved model, read it with get_graph, edit it and pass it as graph. A run by graph_id needs an account, because a saved model belongs to one (without one it is refused with account_required). Every run made with an account, inline or by graph_id, is kept and list_runs lists it; a run by graph_id is also filed under its saved model. To run a model again, for example with more trials, call this tool again with the same graph or graph_id and the new trials. get_simulation_results never runs anything: it only reads a run that already happened, and no tool re-runs a run_id. A run that takes longer than about 40 seconds (150 seconds without an account) keeps running in the background: you get status running and a run_id, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the result. Cost: one run per call. Without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that -- a larger model, or a day whose free runs are used up -- 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one (a large run is any run over 100,000 trials x nodes x periods), currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing. A run that starts and then fails mid-run also costs nothing, with or without an account: no credits are charged, and a free run goes back into today's allowance.

graph.description: The model. A model has four parts. root_nodes are the uncertain inputs; each one draws a value from a probability distribution in every trial. calc_nodes are formulas that combine values. edges are links that carry a value from one node to another; a formula refers to its incoming edges by id, like {e1} * {e2}. run_params sets how many trials (random samples) and time periods to simulate. A time period is whatever unit the model's author chooses, such as a month, quarter or year. run_params.time_periods is a count, while time_period arguments and output_request.time_periods are indices counted from 0: with 12 monthly periods, index 11 is month 12. Formula syntax is described on calc_nodes[].formula. Common distributions and their parameters: normal{mean,std}, log_normal{mu,sigma}, uniform{low,high}, triangle{min_val,max_val,mode_val}, beta{alpha,beta}, poisson{lambda_val}, bernoulli{p}. Leave graph_id out when you send this.

graph_id.description: The id of a model you saved, from save_graph or list_graphs, to run that model instead of sending it inline. Its current version runs, with the run settings saved with it unless trials is given. Leave graph out when you send this. Requires a Neumann account -- an anonymous caller must use graph instead. If an input in the saved model has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model and costs nothing.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

trials.description: Optional. How many trials to run this time (a trial count), in place of the model's run_params.trials, for a model inline or saved. (get_simulation_results' trials is a page of trial rows instead.) It applies to this run only and never changes a saved model. The same trial limits and price apply as to a model sent with that many trials.
trials.title: Trials

seed.description: Optional whole number that fixes the random draws, so repeating the call gives the same result. Exact repeats are guaranteed only for small runs, where trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000.
seed.title: Seed

detail.description: How much to return. summary (the default): the output nodes' mean, 10th/50th/90th percentiles, minimum and maximum, a compact per-period series, and your metrics. full: every node and edge in every period with histograms; when that comes to more than 45,000 characters, the most one tool result is allowed to carry, it is cut down to fit (histograms first, then edges, other nodes and periods) and truncation lists what was left out. summary is never cut. Prefer summary, then ask get_simulation_results for the specific numbers you need.
detail.title: Detail

AggregationRequest.description: A financial metric computed over one node's whole time series in every trial, then summarized as a distribution. Available: npv (net present value), irr (internal rate of return), mirr (modified IRR), payback and discounted_payback (periods until cumulative cash turns positive), cagr (compound annual growth rate), cumsum (running total), terminal_value, and prob (the chance a value passes a threshold). Discounting counts periods from 0: the first period is not discounted. Model an up-front investment as a negative value in period 0. Do not also discount inside the node's formula with PV() or DISCOUNT(), which count from 1, or the first period is discounted twice. cumsum gives one number per trial: the total of the node's values over every simulated period. output_request.time_periods does not shorten it. prob can target any earlier metric, including npv and cumsum. Its mean in the result is the probability, the share of trials that pass. A prob that targets a node directly only tests the node's final-period value. Recipe for the chance that a cumulative total over the first N periods beats X: add {id: total, function: cumsum, target_node_id: <node>}, then {id: p, function: prob, target_aggregation_id: total, params: {op: '>', value: X}}, and read aggregations.p.basic_stats.mean. This works directly when the model has exactly N periods. If it has more, point cumsum at a calc node with formula IF({time_period} <= N, {e1}, 0). {time_period} counts from 1. Use cumsum and prob for totals and probabilities here. A running-total node is needed only for rank_inputs_by_impact and summarize_outcome_scenarios, which measure one node in one period.

id.description: Name for this metric in the result. Must be unique.
id.title: Id

target_node_id.description: The node whose time series the metric uses. Needed for every metric except a prob that uses target_aggregation_id. A prob sets exactly one of the two.
target_node_id.title: Target Node Id

target_aggregation_id.description: Only for prob: the id of a metric listed earlier in this request (for example an npv or cumsum) whose per-trial values are tested against the threshold.
target_aggregation_id.title: Target Aggregation Id

function.description: One of npv, irr, mirr, payback, discounted_payback, cagr, cumsum, terminal_value, prob. npv needs rate, a decimal per period (0.01 is 1%), so a model with monthly periods needs a monthly rate (10% a year is about 0.008 a month); or rates, a list of per-period decimals with at least one entry per period; the first entry is ignored because period 0 is not discounted. discounted_payback needs rate. terminal_value needs g (growth) and rate. mirr needs finance_rate and reinvest_rate. prob needs op (>, >=, <, <=, ==) and value.

params.description: The metric's settings, for example {"rate": 0.1} for npv, {"op": ">", "value": 0} for prob, {"g": 0.02, "rate": 0.1} for terminal_value.

CalcNode.description: A formula node. Its formula combines the values on its incoming edges. There is no automatic sum: write {e1}+{e2} to add two edges, or {e1} to pass one through. A node with no formula is always 0, and check_simulation_model reports that as a warning.

formula.description: Expression over incoming edge ids in braces, for example '{e1} * 0.5 + {e2}'. Leave it out only if the node should always be 0. Operators: + - * / ^ (power) and parentheses; dividing by zero gives 0. Comparisons == != < <= > >= work inside IF. Functions (any case): MIN, MAX, ROUND, ABS, POW, SQRT, LOG, LN, EXP, FLOOR, CEIL, SUM, PRODUCT, AVERAGE, MEAN, IF(condition, then, else), AND, OR, NOT, PV(rate, value, period), DISCOUNT(rate, period), BINOMIAL, INDEX(edge, k) for the k-th item (from 1) of a list value, LENGTH. Special values: {time_period} is the current period counted from 1 (unlike the 0-based time_period arguments), {is_first} and {is_last} are 1 on the first or last period and 0 otherwise.

tools.name: rank_inputs_by_impact
tools.description: Ranks a model's uncertain inputs by how much each one moves a chosen outcome, and returns the data for a tornado chart (a bar chart with one horizontal bar per input, the biggest swing at the top). This is a one-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity analysis: it shows how much the outcome changes when each input changes on its own. Every input is held at its median while one input at a time is set to low, middle and high values from its own distribution (by default its 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles). The tool records how the outcome's average changes. Use this when you need to know which assumption matters most, so you know what to research or de-risk first. It returns one entry per input, ranked so rank 1 has the biggest impact. Each entry lists the input values tried, the outcome at each, and an elasticity score. Elasticity is about how many percent the outcome's average moves when the input moves 1 percent, averaged over the values tried. It is never negative: it says how much an input matters, not which way it pushes the outcome. For the direction, compare outcome_at_low with outcome_at_high: if the outcome is higher at the input's high value, the input pushes it up. When the outcome's average is near zero, percent changes become very large and elasticity is not a useful measure: compare outcome_at_low, outcome_at_high and the swing between them instead. It returns numbers, not an image. Inputs whose distribution produces a list of values are skipped. It takes the model inline in graph, or a saved model by graph_id, so call it directly when the user asks about a saved model, even one that may be unfinished: if an input has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model, which names every such input and costs nothing, so the refusal itself tells you what to fix. An analysis that starts returns a run_id. It runs the model once per input per value tried, so on a big model it can take minutes: if it is not done in about 40 seconds (150 seconds without an account) you get status running, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the ranking. Cost: it counts as one run per call, however many times it runs the model inside, and it is charged only if the analysis succeeds. Without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that, 1 credit for a small model or 5 for a large one (a large model is any model over 100,000 trials x nodes x periods), currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing, and so is a saved graph refused with incomplete_model: no credit, no free run, no run recorded. An analysis that starts and then fails partway through also costs nothing, with or without an account: no credits are charged, and a free run goes back into today's allowance.

target_node_id.description: The id of the outcome node to measure. Defaults to the last calc node in the model, which is usually the final outcome.

time_period.description: Index of the time period to measure, counting from 0: with 12 monthly periods, 11 is month 12. Defaults to the last period. tools.name: summarize_outcome_scenarios

Default [0, 0.5, 1]: 0 is the lowest trial (labelled worst), 0.5 the median, and 1 the highest trial (labelled best). Other values are labelled like p10 (10th percentile). Values between 0 and 1 are estimated from a histogram. The labels assume higher is better: for a cost or a duration, 'worst' is the lowest (cheapest or fastest) trial, so ask for percentiles such as 0.1 and 0.9 and read them as low and high.
percentiles.title: Percentiles

seed.description: Optional whole number that fixes the random draws, so repeating the call gives the same result. Exact repeats are guaranteed only for small runs, where trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000.
seed.title: Seed

tools.name: check_simulation_model
tools.description: Checks a model you hold inline for mistakes, before you save or run it, and lists every problem it finds. It looks for loops with no delay, nodes that are not connected, unknown distributions, missing or invalid distribution parameters, and broken formulas. A loop, including an edge from a node to itself, is allowed and is not an error when at least one edge in it has delay 1 or more. Use this when you have built or edited a model and want to fix it without spending a run. It takes the model inline, not a graph_id: to check a saved model, read it with get_graph and pass what that returns. It does not run or rank anything, and it does not say what a run will cost (use estimate_simulation_size_and_cost for that). It returns is_valid and a list of issues. A draft input with no distribution yet (distribution_type null) is not rejected: it comes back as an issue with severity error naming that input, and is_valid is false, so the model is not ready to run until each such input has a distribution. You do not need this tool to learn that an input with only a low-high guess cannot run: it cannot, and convert_range_to_distribution turns the guess into a distribution. Each issue gives the rule broken, a severity (error, warning or info, where info is only a note), a message, and the node and edge ids involved. If an edge points at a node that does not exist, or the model is over your tier's size limit, you get an error message instead of the list. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs. Without an account, a model over 1,000 trials or 20 nodes is rejected, also at no cost.

graph.description: The model: root_nodes (uncertain inputs), calc_nodes (formulas), edges (links; formulas refer to them like {e1}) and run_params (trials and time periods). Same format as run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph, which documents formulas, periods, distributions and financial metrics in full. Unlike there, an input may have no distribution yet (distribution_type null, distribution_params {}): it is reported as an error, not rejected. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

tools.name: estimate_simulation_size_and_cost
tools.description: Predicts how large a run of a model will be and how many credits it will cost, without running it. Use this before running a large or unfamiliar model, or to check that an account can afford it. It does not tell you whether a model is ready to run and does not list its mistakes: for that use check_simulation_model, and for a saved model read it with get_graph first. It returns the number of trials, time periods, nodes and edges, the estimated peak memory in MB, a complexity score, the size tier (small or large), the credit cost for an account, and a rough run time in seconds for run_monte_carlo_simulation and for rank_inputs_by_impact (which runs the model many times). Runs over about 40 seconds (150 seconds without an account) continue in the background and are collected with get_simulation_results. A run is small when trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000, and large otherwise. With an account there is no fixed trial or node cap: the free-run limits below decide only whether a run is free, and a model beyond them is simply charged in credits. That cost is what run_monte_carlo_simulation, summarize_outcome_scenarios and rank_inputs_by_impact each charge for this model. It needs a model it can size: if the model cannot be read (for example an input whose distribution_type is null), it returns that error instead of an estimate, but it is not a check, so a model it sizes can still have mistakes. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs. Without an account, a model over 1,000 trials or 20 nodes is rejected, also at no cost.

graph.description: The model: root_nodes (uncertain inputs), calc_nodes (formulas), edges (links; formulas refer to them like {e1}) and run_params (trials and time periods). Same format as run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph, which documents formulas, periods, distributions and financial metrics in full. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

tools.name: convert_range_to_distribution
tools.description: Turns a low-to-high guess, such as "between 80 and 120, 90% sure", into the exact parameters a model input needs. A distribution is the shape of the uncertainty, for example normal (a bell curve), log_normal (skewed and never negative), triangle or uniform. The low and high values are the edges of the range you are that sure of, not hard limits. Use this when you have a rough estimate and need distribution parameters instead of guessing them: an input with only a low-high guess has no distribution yet and cannot run until it has one. You do not need it for a three-point low / most likely / high estimate: that goes straight into the model as a triangle input (min_val, mode_val, max_val), so call run_monte_carlo_simulation directly. Its reverse is convert_distribution_to_range. It returns the distribution type and its parameters, ready to use as a model input's distribution_params. The distribution_type parameter explains which type fits which kind of quantity. Supported types: normal, log_normal, uniform, triangle, beta, gamma, exponential, binomial, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal, discrete_gamma, constant and bernoulli. Not supported: poisson, categorical, dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array. For beta, give low and high as fractions (2% is 0.02). Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

distribution_type.description: The distribution to fit. Which to pick: a rate or proportion between 0 and 1 (conversion, churn) → beta, with low and high given as fractions (2% is 0.02). A positive amount that can run high (revenue, price, deal size) → log_normal. A quantity equally likely to land above or below its middle → normal. A value with hard limits you know → uniform (flat) or triangle (most likely value in between). A whole-number count (customers, units) → discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal or discrete_gamma, or binomial for successes out of a fixed number of attempts. Not supported here: poisson, categorical, dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

min_estimate.description: The low end of your range. Required for every type except constant and bernoulli. Exponential ignores it, but a value must still be sent (any number works).
min_estimate.title: Min Estimate

max_estimate.description: The high end of your range. Required for every type except constant and bernoulli.
max_estimate.title: Max Estimate

percentile_range.description: A single fraction: the share of outcomes that should fall between the low and high ends, which is how sure you are. The default 0.9 means the middle 90%: a 5% chance of being below the low end and 5% above the high end. Mapping hedged words: "very sure" or "almost certainly" is about 0.9; "probably" is about 0.8; if unsure, ask the user. "Could be higher" means pick a right-skewed type such as log_normal, not a wider range.
percentile_range.title: Percentile Range

mode_estimate.description: The most likely value. Required for constant (the fixed value), bernoulli (the chance of success, from 0 to 1) and binomial. For triangle it sets the peak; it must lie strictly between low and high, and defaults to their midpoint. For beta it is used as the peak when a fit allows, but the low and high ends take priority. Ignored by other types.
mode_estimate.title: Mode Estimate

tools.name: convert_distribution_to_range
tools.description: Turns a distribution's parameters into the low and high ends of the range that holds a chosen share of outcomes, by default the middle 90%. It also gives the mean, median, mode, standard deviation and any percentiles you ask for. If you give a threshold, it gives the chance of landing below and above it. Use this when you have distribution parameters, from a model or from fermi (a companion forecasting server from Kromatic, the company behind Neumann; each fermi estimate carries a ready-made model input in next_steps.simulate.root_node, whose distribution_type and distribution_params you can pass here), and want to know what they mean in plain numbers. It accepts every distribution type in neumann://catalog, including types convert_range_to_distribution cannot fit, such as poisson and categorical. Its reverse is convert_range_to_distribution, and a range it returns can be passed straight back to it. Values that do not apply come back as null with a note explaining why, which is not an error: a uniform distribution's mode, or the range itself for a type with no single central range, such as categorical. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

distribution_type.description: The distribution's name. Accepts every type a model input accepts: normal, log_normal, uniform, triangle, beta (values are fractions from 0 to 1), gamma, exponential, poisson, bernoulli, binomial, categorical, constant, discrete_normal, discrete_lognormal and discrete_gamma. categorical returns no range. dirichlet, multivariate_normal and constant_array produce lists of values, so every number comes back null. This is wider than convert_range_to_distribution, which cannot fit poisson or categorical.
distribution_type.title: Distribution Type

distribution_params.description: The distribution's parameters, in the same form a model input uses, for example {"mean": 100, "std": 15} for normal or {"mu": 9.2, "sigma": 0.6} for log_normal.
distribution_params.title: Distribution Params

percentile_range.description: A single fraction: the share of outcomes the returned range should hold, centred on the median. The default 0.9 means the middle 90%, so the range runs from the 5th to the 95th percentile.
percentile_range.title: Percentile Range

quantiles.description: A list of percentiles to report. Each is a fraction from 0 to 1: 0.05 is the 5th percentile, the value 5% of outcomes fall below. No repeats. Default [0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.95], returned under keys p5, p10, p50, p90 and p95.
quantiles.title: Quantiles

threshold.description: Optional value to compare against. The result gives the chance of being at or below it and the chance of being above it. For whole-number distributions it gives the chance of being below and above it, and notes the chance of landing exactly on it.
threshold.title: Threshold

tools.name: get_simulation_results
tools.description: Checks on, and reads, a run you started with run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios, using its run_id (list_runs finds the run_id of an earlier run). Use this when a run tool returned status running or queued: it waits up to 30 seconds for the run to finish, then returns its status and percent done, or the finished result, so call it again until status is completed. Use it also to get specific numbers from a finished simulation without running it again (a finished run keeps every node's and edge's statistics for every period): pass nodes (node, edge or metric ids), periods, percentiles such as 0.05 or 0.95, a threshold to get the chance a value is at least or at most some number, or histogram for the distribution's shape. Without those it returns the summary (or the ranking, or the scenarios). Only a simulation made with an account (run_monte_carlo_simulation, with the model inline or by graph_id) keeps every trial. For such a run, percentiles and threshold are counted over every trial, and query.method says exact. Every other run (one made without an account, any rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios run, and the rare run whose trials could not be stored) keeps only its summary statistics and a 64-bin histogram (trial counts in 64 value ranges): its percentiles and threshold are estimates, query.method says histogram, and it cannot return trials (per_trial_not_kept). The estimate is close for a bell-shaped result (under 0.2% error for a normal distribution) but can be far off for a skewed one (a log-normal median read 1.80, exact 1.00). For individual trials of a run that kept them, ask for trial rows: pass trials {start, count} with nodes (here trials is a page of rows to read, not a trial count): query.trials has one row per trial with its value for each node and period, enough to work out how correlated two nodes were across trials. A page holds at most 500 trials and 10,000 values; a larger request is refused with the largest count that fits. This tool only reads a run that already happened and never runs the model again: to run the same model again, for example with more trials, call run_monte_carlo_simulation with the model, or with the saved model's graph_id and trials. For a run you made, the model it ran is in the model field, so you can pass that if the model is no longer in the conversation. A failed run returns its error and is not charged. Only the caller who started the run can read it, and only with the run_id, which is returned to that caller alone. A run started without an account can be read for 24 hours and only from the same network address and client, because a caller without an account is recognized by them; sign in with a free Kromatic account for runs that are not tied to one connection. Credentials go in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential; no Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

run_id.description: The run_id returned by run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios, or listed by list_runs.
run_id.title: Run Id

wait_seconds.description: If the run is still going, wait up to this many seconds (0 to 50, default 30) for it to finish before answering. Returns as soon as it finishes. 0 answers at once with the current percent done.
wait_seconds.title: Wait Seconds

nodes.description: Ids of the nodes, edges or metrics (output_request.aggregations ids) to return numbers for. Default: the output nodes.
nodes.title: Nodes

periods.description: Time period indices to return, counting from 0. Default: the last period only. Ignored for metrics, which cover the whole run.
periods.title: Periods

period_from.description: Instead of periods: the first index of a range of periods.
period_from.title: Period From

period_to.description: Instead of periods: the last index of a range (inclusive).
period_to.title: Period To

percentiles.description: Percentiles to return, as fractions from 0 to 1 (0.95 is the 95th percentile). Default [0.1, 0.5, 0.9].
percentiles.title: Percentiles

threshold.description: A value to test: returns, for each node and period, the chance (0 to 1) that it is at least this value (or at most it, see threshold_direction), for example the chance cash is at least 0 in month 6.
threshold.title: Threshold

threshold_direction.description: at_least (default): the chance of being greater than or equal to threshold. at_most: the chance of being less than or equal to it.
threshold_direction.title: Threshold Direction

histogram.description: true to also return a histogram (trial counts per value bin) for up to 3 of the rows.
histogram.title: Histogram

trials.description: A page of trial rows: individual trials of a finished run, one row each. start is the first trial's index (from 0); count is how many rows, not how many trials to run (this tool never runs anything). Needs nodes; periods default to the last. Page on with a larger start.

TrialsRequest.description: Which page of individual trials to return.

start.description: Index of the first trial, from 0.

tools.name: check_account_and_credits
tools.description: Shows who Neumann thinks you are and what you can still do: your free runs left today and when they reset, and your credit balance if you have an account. Use this when you need to know, before or after a run, whether the next call will be free or spend credits, how much is left, or whether you are signed in -- and when a run was refused for want of runs or credits, so you can tell the user which it was. There are three tiers. Without an account you get 3 free runs per UTC day; you are recognized by network address and client, so on a hosted platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT many callers share one identity and today's free runs may already be spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account you get your own 10 free runs per UTC day, spent before any credits. After those, runs cost credits. An account created with POST https://neumann.kromatic.com/api/v1/accounts authenticates you and starts with 5 free credits, but it carries no free daily runs -- only signing in with a Kromatic account does. It returns whether you are anonymous or an account, your account id and status, credit balance, free runs left today with the reset time and the size limits that apply to you, the price of one credit in US dollars, and your last 10 credit transactions. With an account it also returns how many models are saved on your account and the three most recently updated, each with its graph_id, so when the user mentions a saved model you can often go straight to get_graph without calling list_graphs. Credentials go in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential and nowhere else; no Neumann tool takes an api_key argument, and a credential that is not recognized returns an unauthorized error. This tool itself needs no account -- it is how a caller without one finds that out. Setup docs: https://kromatic.com/mcp/neumann. Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

tools.name: send_feedback
tools.description: Sends a short report about Neumann to the team that builds it. Use this when the user wants to report a problem, a wrong result, a confusing message or a missing feature (including asking you to pass a request or suggestion on to the team), or has agreed to your offer to send one. Send only after the user agrees: when a tool fails, first tell the user what happened and ask, and do not call this tool until they say yes. Good moments to offer: a tool returned an error or a result that looks wrong, the user needed something Neumann could not do, or the work with Neumann is wrapping up and the user might want to say what worked. Offer it as a question, for example: 'Want me to send Neumann's team a short note about this?' The team reads every report. Do not offer after each routine successful call. Put several points in one report: a signed-in account may send 5 per hour and 20 per day, and callers without an account share 60 per hour and 300 per day. Only message is required. Fill in the other fields that apply so the team can act without guessing. Write in your own words. Never include personal data (names, email addresses, company names), the user's own numbers (inputs or results), secrets or keys, or the conversation transcript; describe the task and any wrong result in general terms instead. Add sender_email only if the user wants a reply. If you are signed in, your account id is included. No account is needed. It returns status "sent". Cost: free, with or without an account -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs.

message.description: The report, in your own words, 10 to 5,000 characters. Say what you tried, what happened and what you expected. Leave out names, companies, the user's numbers (inputs or results) and the conversation itself: write "a revenue forecast", not its figures.
message.title: Message
examples: rank_inputs_by_impact returned an empty list for a model with two inputs, so I could not tell the user which one mattered more.

feedback_type.description: What kind of report this is. bug: a tool errored or broke. wrong_result: it ran but the numbers look wrong. unmet_use_case: the user needed something no tool does. feature_request: a missing option or parameter. confusing: a description, output or error was hard to understand. praise: something worked well. other: anything else (the default).
feedback_type.title: Feedback Type

tool_name.description: The Neumann tool the report is about, for example run_monte_carlo_simulation.
tool_name.title: Tool Name

run_id.description: The run_id the report is about, if a run was involved.
run_id.title: Run Id

user_goal.description: What the user was trying to do, as a general task in a few words, for example "estimate a project budget". No names, company names or figures.
user_goal.title: User Goal

what_happened.description: What actually happened, in general terms, without the user's numbers.
what_happened.title: What Happened

expected.description: What you expected to happen instead.
expected.title: Expected

error_text.description: The error code and message the tool returned, if any. Remove any personal data or user figures it quotes.
error_text.title: Error Text

suggestion.description: What would have helped: a fix, a new feature or clearer wording.
suggestion.title: Suggestion

impact.description: How much it cost the user. blocked: could not finish. workaround: finished another way. minor: an annoyance. none: no cost, for example praise.
impact.title: Impact

sender_email.description: Optional. The user's email address, only if they want a reply and gave it to you. Do not invent one. No copy is sent to it.
sender_email.title: Sender Email

tools.name: buy_credits
tools.description: Charges the payment card saved on the user's account to buy Neumann credits; without a saved card it charges nothing and returns a checkout link instead. One call buys at most 100 credits ($50.00 at the price in the Cost line below). When the user asks for more than 100: do not call this tool yet, not even for 100. Tell the user that one purchase is at most 100 credits and ask how many to buy now, up to 100; call it once they name an amount within the limit. Each purchase, including a second one, needs the user's agreement to its amount. (A call asking for more than 100 would be refused and charge nothing.) Credits pay for runs once the free runs for the day are used up, or for a model too large to run free. Use this when an account is low on credits and the user has agreed to the purchase; to see the balance and the live price first, call check_account_and_credits. When no card is saved yet, it returns payment_status checkout_required and a checkout_url, which the user opens in a browser to save a card before you call this tool again. It returns the credits bought, the new balance, the payment status and, when a card is needed, the checkout_url. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. When you are signed in rather than using a key, the sign-in must also include billing access: a permission, the OAuth scope named neumann:billing, that lets a sign-in spend money on the account and that the user grants when signing in. A key does not need it. Without it the call is refused with insufficient_scope and charges nothing; the user signs in again and grants billing access. Cost: charges the payment card saved on your account for each credit, currently $0.50 per credit (check_account_and_credits shows the live price). It needs an account, and credits are what a run costs once your free runs for the day are gone -- 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one.

credits.description: How many credits to buy: at least 1 and at most 100 in one call.
credits.title: Credits

tools.name: create_result_share_link
tools.description: Creates a public web link to one of your results, so you can hand the numbers to someone who has no Neumann account. Use this when the user wants to send, publish or show a result to another person; to put the numbers in the conversation instead, call get_simulation_results. It works for any run you own: a run from run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios, including a run of a graph you saved. There is one share tool for every kind of run -- do not look for a separate one. To give someone the model itself, so they can work on it, call create_model_share_link instead. Pass the run_id the run tool returned when the run was made; for a run made earlier, in another conversation, find its run_id with list_runs. You do not need a graph_id. That holds for a run of a saved model too: when the user asks to share the run of a saved graph, call this tool directly with that run's run_id -- list_graphs and get_graph return graph_ids, not run_ids, so they are not a step here. Calling it again for the same run returns the same link rather than a second one. Anyone who has the link can open the result without signing in, so ask the user before you create one. To turn a link off and keep the result, call revoke_share_link; calling this tool again afterwards issues a fresh link, and the old one stays dead. delete_run deletes the result, and so its link too. A run made without an account takes two calls, and the run_id is what carries it from one to the other. First call: the caller has no account, so call this tool with the run_id anyway; nothing is shared, and it returns a message asking the user to sign in with a free Kromatic account -- tell the user that. Second call: once the user has signed in, call this tool again with the SAME run_id. Only that second call shares the run and keeps it on the account; signing in alone shares nothing, and a different run_id, or a new run, does not carry the claim. Do it within 24 hours, because a run made without an account is deleted after that. When you tell the user what happens next, say both steps: sign in, then you will share it using the same run. It returns the share_url. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets authentication_required.

run_id.description: The run to share, as returned by any run tool. For a run made without an account, sign in and then call again with this same run_id: signing in alone shares nothing.
run_id.title: Run Id

tools.name: revoke_share_link
tools.description: Turns off the public link to one of your results, or the share token of one of your saved models, and keeps the result or the model: nothing is deleted, and it can be shared again. Use this when the user wants something they shared to stop working but wants to keep it. For a result's link, pass the run_id of the shared result (not the link). For a model's share token, pass the graph_id of the model you shared with create_model_share_link (not the token). Pass one of the two, not both. When the user wants the result itself removed, use delete_run instead: it deletes the result and its link. From then on anyone who opens the old link, or passes the old token to get_graph, gets "not found", and it never works again, even if you share again. That cannot be undone for the people who hold the old link or token, and it is why this tool is marked destructive; the result or model itself is kept. A copy someone already saved with save_graph is theirs and is not affected. It returns revoked true, or false when there was no active link or token, so calling it again is harmless. To share again, call create_result_share_link or create_model_share_link: each makes a new link or token. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

run_id.description: The run whose public link to turn off, as passed to create_result_share_link. The result is kept. Omit it when you pass graph_id.
run_id.title: Run Id

graph_id.description: The saved graph whose share token to turn off, as passed to create_model_share_link. The model is kept. Omit it when you pass run_id.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

tools.name: create_model_share_link
tools.description: Shares one of your saved models with another person who has a Neumann account, so they can work on it: they can read it, run it and save their own copy to change, but they cannot change yours. It returns a token, not a web page. A saved model is called a graph. Use this when the user wants to send or hand over the model itself -- its inputs, estimates, formulas and details -- so someone else can work on it. To share a result (the numbers from a run) instead, call create_result_share_link with the run_id: that makes a web page anyone can open, while this returns a token only a signed-in account can use, with no web page. Pass the graph_id from save_graph or list_graphs. It returns share_token: give it to the other person. They call get_graph with share_token to read the model as it is currently saved, without your graph_id; they can run it, or save their own copy with save_graph and no graph_id. They cannot change your model, and their copy does not change when you edit yours. The token always reads your latest saved version, not a snapshot: to share the model as it is now while you keep editing, save a copy first (save_graph with no graph_id) and share the copy. Calling it again for the same graph returns the same token. To turn the token off, call revoke_share_link with the graph_id; delete_graph turns it off too, and restoring the graph does not turn it back on. Sharing again afterwards makes a new token. Neumann has no teams, invitations or shared editing: each account works on its own copy. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

graph_id.description: Which of your saved graphs to share, from save_graph or list_graphs.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

tools.name: save_graph
tools.description: Saves a model to your Neumann account so you can come back to it instead of describing it again. A saved model is called a graph: its uncertain inputs, the formulas that combine them, and the links between them. Use this when the user will revisit this model -- a budget, a plan, a business case they will update -- or when you want to re-analyse it later without resending it; for a one-off question, pass the model inline to run_monte_carlo_simulation and save nothing. Omit graph_id to save a new graph. Pass the graph_id of a graph you saved before to replace that same graph with this version; the earlier versions are kept, so replacing is not losing anything. Every save stores a new version: give version_name to label it, list_graph_versions lists the versions, and get_graph reads any of them. An input may be saved before it has a distribution, so you can build a draft model over a conversation; a graph with such an input cannot be run or analysed until each input has one. An input can also be given as an estimated range (estimate: worst, best, most likely) with a distribution_type and no params: the save fits the params to the range. Changing a saved input's range re-fits its params, and changing only its params works the range out again. If a range cannot be fitted, the error estimate_fit_failed names the input and nothing at all is saved: not that input, not the rest of the model, and a graph you were replacing keeps its last saved version. So after that error there is nothing new to read back with get_graph; tell the user which range could not be fitted and fix it. What the model means is kept with it: its details (description, tags, time unit, start date, goal), each node's unit and description, and the metrics it asks for in run_params.output_request. A goal on a node the model does not have is refused with unknown_node, and nothing is saved. It returns the graph_id to use later, the version_id of the version it just stored, the name, and when it was last updated. Use that graph_id with run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact or summarize_outcome_scenarios in place of an inline graph, with get_graph to read it back, and with delete_graph to remove it. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

graph.description: The model to save: its uncertain inputs (root_nodes), the formulas over them (calc_nodes), the links between them (edges) and the run settings (run_params). The same shape run_monte_carlo_simulation takes, except that an input may be saved before it has a distribution: give it distribution_type null and distribution_params {}. A graph with such an input cannot be run until you give it one. An input may also carry an estimate, the range behind it (worst, best, mode): send a range and a distribution_type without params and the params are fitted to the range on save; send only params and the range they imply is stored. Leave estimate out to keep the one already saved. details, each node's unit and description, and run_params.output_request are kept as sent. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

tools.name: list_graphs
tools.description: Lists the graphs saved on your Neumann account, the most recently updated first. Use this when the user refers to a saved model that is not among the newest ones check_account_and_credits shows, or to page through all of them; it is how you find the graph_id that get_graph, run_monte_carlo_simulation, rank_inputs_by_impact, summarize_outcome_scenarios and delete_graph take. It does not list runs or results (that is list_runs) -- it lists the models themselves. It returns one entry per graph with its graph_id, name, when it was last updated and how many input and formula nodes it has, plus next_offset when there are more to page through. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

tools.name: get_graph
tools.description: Reads one graph you saved earlier, by its graph_id, or a graph another account shared with you, by its share_token, and returns the whole model in the same shape the run tools accept; an input saved without a distribution comes back with distribution_type null and distribution_params {}. Use this when you want to show the user what is in a saved model, or edit it before running it again: pass the edited model to run_monte_carlo_simulation as graph. To run a saved model unchanged, or with only a different trial count, you do not need this tool: call run_monte_carlo_simulation with its graph_id (and trials). To find a graph_id first, call list_graphs. It returns the graph_id, the name, when it was last updated, and the graph itself: its uncertain inputs with their distributions, the formula nodes, the links between them and the run settings with the metrics it asks for, plus its details and each node's unit and description, as saved, and the version number of what it returned. Pass version, a number from list_graph_versions, to read that earlier version instead of the current model: it comes back in the same shape, with the run settings and details it was saved with. Reading an earlier version changes nothing; to restore one, follow the steps in list_graph_versions. To read a model someone shared with you, pass share_token (the token they got from create_model_share_link, or a link containing it) instead of graph_id: it returns their model as currently saved, with graph_id null, and version cannot be used with it. You cannot change their model; run it by passing it to run_monte_carlo_simulation as graph, or keep your own copy with save_graph and no graph_id. It reads the model, not any result of running it. After a save_graph error nothing new was saved, so this returns the graph as it was before that call. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

tools.name: list_graph_versions
tools.description: Lists the saved versions of one graph on your Neumann account, newest first. Every save_graph call stores a new version of the graph it saves, so this is that model's history. Use this when the user wants to see how a saved model has changed, find an earlier version of it, or go back to how it was before -- for example, how the model looked last week. It returns one entry per version with its version number (the number get_graph's version takes), its version_id, when it was saved, the label given with save_graph's version_name (null when none was given) and how many nodes it had, plus next_offset when there are more to page through. To read a version, pass its number to get_graph as version. To restore a version, take two steps: first read it with get_graph and that version number; then save the graph get_graph returned with save_graph and the same graph_id. Only the save_graph step writes anything: the restored model becomes the current one and is stored as a new version, so no version is lost. A single version cannot be deleted: delete_graph deletes the whole model, every version with it. It lists one model's versions, not your other models (that is list_graphs) and not runs or results. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

tools.name: list_runs
tools.description: Lists the runs on your Neumann account, the most recently started first. Every run made with an account is kept and listed here: run_monte_carlo_simulation (inline or by graph_id), rank_inputs_by_impact and summarize_outcome_scenarios runs alike. Use this when the user refers to a result from earlier and you do not have its run_id, for example after the conversation that made it has ended. Pass graph_id to list only the runs of one saved model, or kind to list only one kind of run. It returns one entry per run with its run_id, its kind, the saved model it came from (none for a model passed inline), its status, when it started and finished, how many trials it ran and, for a simulation, one median to tell runs apart, plus next_offset when there are more to page through. To read a run's results, pass its run_id to get_simulation_results. It lists runs, not models (that is list_graphs), and not deleted runs (that is list_deleted). A run made without an account is not listed. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Example: {"limit":20,"offset":0} Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

tools.name: export_run
tools.description: Gives you one of your finished runs as a file of every trial, as a CSV, and returns a temporary download link. Use this when the user wants the raw data as a file: all the trials of a run to open in a spreadsheet such as Excel or Google Sheets, or to hand to someone. The file has one row per trial: a trial column (counting from 0), then one column per node and period, named like "revenue [p2]" (the node id, then period 2). Every node and every period is included unless you pass nodes or periods to include only some. The values are the exact values drawn in each trial. It returns download_url, expires_at, rows (the trial count) and columns (the header row). The link needs no credential and expires; call again for a fresh one. Only a simulation made with an account (run_monte_carlo_simulation) keeps its trials; for any other run it returns per_trial_not_kept. To read or analyse trials yourself in the conversation, such as how correlated two nodes were across trials, use get_simulation_results with trials instead: this tool is for handing the data over as a file, not for reading it. It reads a run that already happened and never runs the model again. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

tools.name: delete_graph
tools.description: Deletes one graph you saved, together with the runs of it and every saved version of it; it cannot delete one version and keep the rest. Use this when the user has explicitly asked for that model to be removed, and not otherwise. Confirm which one first with list_graphs or get_graph, because the graph_id is the only thing that says which model goes. It disappears from every tool as soon as this returns. For 30 days it can be restored, with its runs, by restore_deleted (list_deleted shows it); after that it is gone for good. Deleting the same graph twice changes nothing and does not extend the 30 days. To stop using a graph without removing it, just leave it saved and do not pass its graph_id. To turn off only a result's share link and keep the result, use revoke_share_link instead. It returns the graph_id, what kind of thing was deleted, the time it was deleted and the time after which it can no longer be restored. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

A deleted item can be restored for 30 days after it was deleted; after that it no longer appears here and is gone for good. It returns one entry per item with its kind (graph or run), its id, its name when it has one, when it was deleted and the time after which it can no longer be restored, plus next_offset when there are more to page through. Pass kind to list only graphs or only runs. When a saved model is deleted its runs go with it, and restoring the model brings them back. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Example: {"limit":20,"offset":0} Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

tools.name: restore_deleted
tools.description: Restores a saved model or a run you deleted with delete_graph or delete_run, putting it back exactly as it was. Use this when the user wants back something they deleted, within 30 days of deleting it; find its kind and id with list_deleted. Restoring a model brings back the runs that were deleted with it, and their share links work again. A run whose model is still deleted cannot be restored on its own (parent_deleted): restore the model first. After the 30 days it is refused with restore_window_expired and the item cannot be recovered. Restoring something that is not deleted changes nothing. It returns the kind, the id and when it was restored. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Example: {"kind":"graph","id":"8f3c2a"} Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.

Deleting the same run twice changes nothing and does not extend the 30 days. It returns the run_id, what kind of thing was deleted, the time it was deleted and the time after which it can no longer be restored. It needs a Neumann account: send your key, or your signed-in token, in the Authorization header as a Bearer credential. No Neumann tool takes an api_key argument. Cost: free -- it debits no credits and spends none of your free daily runs -- but it needs an account; an anonymous caller gets account_required.
